title: Speed versus Damage
subtitle: Six trade-offs that decide how bad an incident gets, from the first alert to the regulator's clock

intro.question: Where in an incident do minutes matter, where do they not, and what actually shortens the damage?
body: An incident is a race: the attacker spreads, the business bleeds, and deadlines tick. This lab gives you six small models, one for each stage of a response: spotting the real alert among the noise, how far an intruder spreads before you notice, how fast containment works, whether to shut a plant down, how long recovery takes and which legal clocks have already run out.

Every number here is **illustrative**, chosen to show the shape of each trade-off, not to predict a real incident. The deadlines in the last step are real; whether each applies depends on who you are and what was affected.

variables.label: Loss if it reaches the plant
Hours to decide it is material

formulas.label: Expected loss if you keep running

steps.title: More alerts, fewer catches
body: A ((SOC)) receives [[alertsPerDay]] alerts a day. [[analysts]] analysts can each ((triage)) about [[perAnalyst]] alerts properly, so only **{triageShare}** get a real look.
Hidden in the noise are about [[realPerMonth]] real incidents a month. If triage is a lottery, about **{missedPerMonth}** of them slip past each month.

predict.prompt: A new security tool goes live untuned and doubles the alerts to 2,000 a day. Same team. What happens to the real incidents you miss?

options.text: Fewer are missed: more alerts means more coverage.
options.why: Only if someone looks at them. With the same team, extra alerts mostly add noise, so a smaller share of everything gets real attention.

options.text: More are missed: the triaged share halves.
options.why: 400 good triages out of 2,000 alerts is 20%, down from 40%. The real incidents are now buried deeper.

options.text: No change: the team's capacity is the same.
options.why: Capacity is the same, but it is spread over twice as much. The share that gets a proper look drops.

predict.notice: Only **{triageShare}** of alerts get a real look now, and about **{missedPerMonth}** real incidents a month slip past. Tuning detections is as important as adding them.

challenge.prompt: Keep 2,000 alerts a day and find a way to triage every one properly.
challenge.success: {analysts|int} analysts × {perAnalyst|int} alerts covers all {alertsPerDay|int}. In real SOCs this usually comes from tuning and automation, not just hiring.
challenge.hint: Analysts × alerts each has to reach the daily total.

steps.takeaway: Untuned alerts drown real ones; detection quality beats detection quantity.

steps.title: The cost of noticing late
body: An intruder who isn't noticed keeps spreading. In this model the number of compromised machines doubles every [[doublingHours]] hours, out of [[totalHosts]] in the network.
You notice after [[detectHours]] hours. By then **{hostsAtDetect}** machines are compromised. The time between break-in and detection is called ((dwell time)).

visuals.title: Compromised machines over time
visuals.caption: Illustrative: real intruders move in bursts, not smooth doublings. Log scale. Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 puts the global median dwell time at about two weeks.

predict.prompt: Better monitoring halves your detection time, from 72 to 36 hours. How many machines are compromised when you notice?

options.why: Halving the time would halve a steady trickle. Spread compounds, so the saving is much bigger.
36 hours is three doublings instead of six, so 2³ = 8 machines instead of 2⁶ = 64.

options.text: About the same: they're already in
options.why: Getting in is the first step; reaching many machines takes time, and that time is what faster detection takes away.

predict.notice: **{hostsAtDetect}** machines instead of 64. Because spread compounds, every hour you cut from dwell time saves more than the last.

steps.takeaway: Spread compounds, so cutting detection time pays off far more than linearly.

steps.title: Minutes during encryption
body: Once ransomware starts encrypting, it can spread in minutes. Here the encrypted count doubles every [[encMins]] minutes until machines are isolated from the network.
Isolation takes [[containMins]] minutes: finding the right person, getting approval, running the change. **{encrypted}** machines are encrypted before it lands.

visuals.title: Wait for approval, or act on a pre-approved playbook

predict.prompt: Your playbook lets the on-call analyst isolate machines without waiting for a manager, cutting isolation from 120 to 60 minutes. How many machines are spared?

options.why: Halving the time halves the doublings, not the count. Four fewer doublings is 16 times fewer machines.

options.text: None: the damage was done when it started
options.why: Encryption is still spreading while you wait; every doubling you prevent is real machines saved.

predict.notice: **{encrypted}** machines instead of 256. Pre-approved containment, decided calmly in advance, beats a perfect decision made two hours late.

steps.takeaway: Decide containment authority before the incident: during encryption, approval delays cost whole machines per minute.

steps.title: Shut the plant down?
body: Ransomware is in the office network, not the plant. Keep running, and there is a [[pSpread]] chance it reaches the plant's control systems, costing about [[impactIfSpread]] in damage and danger.
Or stop production as a precaution for [[shutdownHours]] at [[costPerHour]] an hour. Expected loss if you run: **{expectedRun}**. Cost of shutting down: **{shutdownCost}**.

visuals.title: Run or shut down?
visuals.caption: A bar marked ! is the worse bet. Real decisions also weigh safety, which no dollar figure fully captures.

predict.prompt: Investigators find the intruder had access to a system that also talks to the plant. The chance of spread rises from 5% to 20%. What now?

options.text: Keep running: a shutdown is a certain loss, spread is only a chance.
options.why: A certain loss feels worse, but at 20% the expected loss of running ($40M here) is more than three times the shutdown's cost.

options.text: Shutting down becomes the better bet.
options.why: 0.20 × $200M = $40M expected loss, against $12M for a five-day precautionary stop.

options.text: It makes no difference to the decision.
options.why: The decision turns on exactly this probability. Quadrupling it flips the answer.

predict.notice: Running now risks **{expectedRun}** against a certain **{shutdownCost}**. This is why some operators stop physical operations while only IT is hit: they can't yet rule out spread, and in a plant the downside includes safety.

challenge.prompt: At a 20% chance of spread, how long could the shutdown last before running becomes the better bet again?
challenge.success: At {shutdownHours|int} hours the shutdown costs {shutdownCost}, at least the {expectedRun} expected loss of running.
challenge.hint: Raise the shutdown length or the hourly cost until the two bars meet.

steps.takeaway: Precautionary OT shutdowns are a bet on uncertainty: the less you can rule out, the more stopping is worth.

steps.title: The bottleneck in recovery
body: Before restoring any machine you need trustworthy ((identity)) systems: the logins and permissions everything else depends on. Rebuilding them takes [[identityHours]] hours, and it can't be parallelised.
Then [[engineers]] engineers restore [[hostsToRestore]] machines at about [[restoreRate]] machines each per hour. Total: **{recoveryHours}**.

predict.prompt: You call in a recovery firm and double the engineers from 10 to 20. How long does recovery now take?

options.why: Only the parallel part halves. The identity rebuild still has to happen first, one step at a time.

options.text: About 73 hours: the identity rebuild still comes first
options.why: 48 h for identity is unchanged; restoring drops from 50 h to 25 h. 48 + 25 = 73.

options.text: No faster: recovery is limited by backups
options.why: Backup speed matters, but here more hands really do shorten the restore part.

predict.notice: **{recoveryHours}**: extra engineers shrank only the teal part. A clean, offline copy of your identity systems is worth more than a second recovery team.

challenge.prompt: Keep 10 engineers and get total recovery under 60 hours.
challenge.success: {recoveryHours} with {engineers|int} engineers. Shrinking the serial step is what did it.
challenge.hint: Which part can't be parallelised? Make it faster, as tested offline identity backups would.

steps.takeaway: Recovery is limited by its serial steps; protect and rehearse identity recovery before you ever need it.

steps.title: The clocks start when you know
body: Regulators set deadlines that start ticking at awareness, not when the investigation ends. Slide [[hoursSince]] forward to see which clocks have run out.
The US SEC clock is different: four business days after the company decides the incident is ((material)), here after [[materialityHours]]. **{clocksMissed|int}** clock(s) have already run out.

visuals.title: Hours left on each clock
visuals.caption: Each rule applies only to certain organisations and incidents. SEC time is approximate (business days, from the materiality decision).

predict.prompt: It is hour 8 of the incident at an Indian company with EU customers. Which clock has already run out?

options.text: None: they all give at least a day.
options.why: Many people assume so, but India's CERT-In directions require reporting within 6 hours of noticing a covered incident.
At hour 8 the CERT-In clock is 2 hours past; NIS2's 24-hour early warning and GDPR's 72 hours are still open.
GDPR allows 72 hours and NIS2 24 hours for the first notice; only the 6-hour clock has passed.

predict.notice: **{clocksMissed|int}** clock run out by hour 8. Fast clocks are why mature teams draft notification templates and know who signs them before anything happens.

steps.takeaway: Notification deadlines start at awareness and can be as short as 6 hours; prepare who reports what, to whom, in advance.

glossary.definition: Security Operations Centre: the team (in-house or outsourced) that watches alerts and handles incidents around the clock.
Quickly sorting alerts into real, harmless or unclear, and deciding what to look at first.
The time between an intruder getting in and the defenders noticing.
The systems that decide who can log in and what they can do, such as Active Directory. Almost everything depends on them, so they are usually restored first.
Important enough that a reasonable investor would want to know. US-listed companies must disclose material cyber incidents to the SEC.

wrapUp.heading: What you discovered
body: Speed matters most where damage compounds: while an intruder spreads and while ransomware encrypts. There, cutting hours of dwell time or minutes of containment saves far more than linearly, which is why teams pre-approve containment and invest in detection quality rather than alert quantity.

Elsewhere, structure matters more than speed. Recovery is held up by serial steps like rebuilding identity. Shutting down a plant is a bet on how much you can rule out. And legal clocks start when you know, so the paperwork has to be ready before the incident.
next: In step 2, set spread to double every 4 hours and see how much a 24-hour detection improvement is worth.
In step 4, make downtime cost $1M an hour and find the spread chance where stopping is worth it.
In step 6, set materiality to 0 hours and watch the SEC clock against the others.
